label: Bhadravyūha
justification: Ācārya Bhadravyūha is a Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin master known exclusively as the author of the Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā (also called Prakīrṇakacaityalakṣaṇa), preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript from Nepal with an anonymous prose commentary (vivecana). While the attribution of the root stanzas and symbolic section to him is accepted (Roth 1980, 1987; Tanemura 2014), his precise dates remain uncertain, established only as antedating Kuladatta's Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā (ca. 11th–12th century CE) which quotes him. | web review: Bhadravyūha is securely identified as the author of the Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā, a Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin text preserved in a single Nepalese manuscript with an anonymous commentary (vivecana). While the manuscript is dated to the 12th or 13th century, the commentary is estimated to date to the early 11th century, and the text is quoted by Kuladatta (11th-12th c. CE). However, Bhadravyūha's exact floruit remains unknown beyond this terminus ante quem, so the status remains X.

label: Vidyāraṇyayati
justification: The Śrīvidyārṇavatantra is a comprehensive Śākta compilation traditionally attributed to a Vidyāraṇyayati, whose lineage in the colophons is given as Govindācārya -> Śaṅkarācārya -> Viṣṇuśarmācārya -> Pragalbhācārya -> Vidyāraṇyayati. Although frequently conflated in popular tradition with the famous 14th-century Advaitin Vidyāraṇya of Vijayanagara, the text postdates Mantramahodadhi (1588), which it quotes, and is found in a manuscript dated 1726, placing the author/compiler between 1588 and 1726. He remains an obscure figure known solely from the colophons of this work, which mandates status X. | web review: The author's identity remains uncertain, as noted by modern scholars (e.g., Gudrun Bühnemann). He is known only from the colophons and lineage of the Śrīvidyārṇavatantra. The date is constrained between 1588 and 1726, but the lack of a settled identity mandates status X.

label: Varuṇaśivācārya
justification: Varuṇaśivācārya is a South Indian Śaivasiddhānta master known as the author of the Vāruṇapaddhati. He quotes Brahmaśambhu (late 11th century) and is commented upon by Nigamajñānadeva in the 16th century, placing him roughly between the 12th and 16th centuries. Because his precise dates remain uncertain beyond this broad interval, status is set to X. | web review: Scholarly sources (such as Dominic Goodall) confirm that Varuṇaśiva's date cannot be precisely determined beyond the broad interval between the mid-to-late 11th century (echoing Somaśambhu and Brahmaśambhu) and the 16th century (when commented upon by Nigamajñānadeva II). As the floruit remains uncertain to within a century, the status remains X.

label: Guṇākara (Śvetāmbara)
justification: Śrī-Śvetāmbara-paṇḍita Guṇākara is a Jaina scholar who authored the Laghuvṛtti commentary on the tantric/magical manual Āścaryayogamālā (traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna; also referred to in relation to the Yogaratnamālā). Pandit 40936 directly corresponds to him, listing his work as 'Yogamālālaguvṛtti'. Filliozat dates his commentary to 1239. He is marked as status X because he is essentially known only from this commentary and colophons. | web review: Scholarly sources (including David Gordon White) confirm Guṇākara was a Śvetāmbara Jaina who composed the Laghuvṛtti on the Āścaryayogamālā (Yogaratnamālā) in 1239 CE (or 1240 CE). Pandit 40936 correctly identifies him and his work. The ATII candidate is an 11th-century Buddhist translator and thus incorrect.

label: Svatantrānandanātha
justification: Svatantrānandanātha is the author of the Śākta/Tantric philosophical treatise Mātṛkācakraviveka, commented upon by Śivānanda (Śivānandamuni). Because Śivānanda is typically placed around the late 12th to 13th century, Svatantrānandanātha must precede him, likely flourishing in the 12th or early 13th century. However, precise biographical details and exact dates remain uncertain, warranting status X. | web review: Svatantrānandanātha is known as the author of the Mātṛkācakraviveka, a Śākta text. His work was commented upon by Śivānanda, who is typically dated to the 12th or 13th century. Consequently, Svatantrānandanātha must have lived before or during this period. However, precise biographical details and exact dates remain uncertain, warranting status X.

label: Alalavajra
candidate_corrections: ATII queries the name as 'Ahovajra?' and 'Vajralala', but Sanskrit manuscripts confirm the reading Ācārya Alalavajra (Tibetan: A la la badzra).
justification: Alalavajra (Tibetan: A la la badzra) is an Indian Vajrayāna master and mahāsiddha belonging to the Hevajra transmission lineages (often situated between Ḍombīheruka and Garbharīpāda / Jayaśrījñāna, or associated with Nandipāda). He authored the Sahajadvibhujahevajrasādhana (attested in Sanskrit manuscript and Tibetan translation) and related works like the Hevajrabalikrama (Tōh. 1298). His precise dates remain approximate (ca. 10th–11th century), hence marked status X. | web review: The identity of Alalavajra is confirmed as the mahāsiddha and disciple of Ḍombīheruka. His date is constrained to the 9th-10th century by his position in the well-documented Hevajra lineage. ATII P3291 is a direct match.

label: Ādiśeṣa
flags: ["soft: web review considers SA_GSP33_ilx_gr_AdizeSa_paramArthasAra pseudepigraphic; move to a pseudo-person?"]
justification: Ādiśeṣa (or Śeṣanāga / Bhagavadaśeṣa) is the traditional author of the original Vaiṣṇava Paramārthasāra (also known as the Ādhārakārikā), a verse treatise combining elements of early Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Advaita-oriented Vedānta, which was famously adapted by Abhinavagupta into Kashmir Śaivism around 1000 CE. Historically, the name Ādiśeṣa reflects a pseudonym or mythologized attribution (often conflated with Patañjali as the serpent incarnation). Based on relative chronology (Danielson 1980 places it after the Āgamaśāstra and before the Yuktidīpikā), modern scholarship dates the text roughly to the 5th–6th century CE. Status is X because the historical persona behind this mythological name remains indeterminate. | web review: The name Ādiśeṣa is a mythological attribution (the divine serpent) for an unknown Vaiṣṇava author of the 5th-6th century CE. Since the historical persona remains indeterminate, the status must remain X.

label: Karavindasvāmin
justification: Karavinda (Karavindasvāmin) is the author of the Śulbapradīpikā (or Śulbadīpikā), a commentary on the Āpastambaśulbasūtra. Chronologically he falls between Kapardisvāmin (c. 11th–12th century) whom he cites/follows and Sundararāja (fl. c. 1500 CE) who cites him; because his floruit cannot yet be pinned down to within a single century, status is X. | web review: Karavindasvāmin's date is bounded by his reliance on Kapardisvāmin (pre-1150 CE) and his being cited by Sundararāja (late 15th century). Scholarly sources do not provide a more precise date, leaving his floruit spanning several centuries. Thus, the status remains X.

label: Anantaśambhu
justification: Anantaśambhu (also referred to as Anantaśivācārya) is the author of the vyākhyā on Trilocanaśivācārya's 12th-century Siddhāntasārāvalī. Modern scholarship (Alexis Sanderson) notes that he quotes Viśvanātha (the 14th-century author of the Siddhāntaśekhara) and Aghoraśiva, thus providing a terminus post quem in the 14th century, but his exact floruit remains otherwise unsettled. | web review: Sources confirm Anantaśambhu's identity as the author of the Siddhāntasārāvalīvyākhyā and match him with Pandit ID 87102. However, his floruit cannot be narrowed down to within a century, as the most recent scholarship (Sanderson) explicitly states that his date is uncertain beyond a terminus post quem of the 14th century.

label: Cannabasaveśvara (Sudhāpura)
justification: Known from the introductory verses of his Vīraśaivotkarṣapradīpikā, Cannabasaveśvara (or Cannabasavārya Deśika) of Sudhāpura is a late Vīraśaiva preceptor. He traces his spiritual lineage after Toṇṭada Siddhamaheśvara (fl. late 15th/early 16th c.) through Murughā Śāntavīra and Gurusiddha Deśika, placing him roughly in the late 17th or 18th century. He must not be confused with the 12th-century Vacanakāra Cannabasava, the nephew of Basaveśvara. | web review: The search confirms that Cannabasaveśvara of Sudhāpura (Swadi) is Swadi Channabasava Swamiji, the successor of Gurusiddha Deśika (Murige Swamiji II) who headed the Murugha Matha until 1729. This securely places his floruit in the mid-18th century. He is the traditional author of the Vīraśaivotkarṣapradīpikā.

label: Giridharācārya
flags: ["soft: date conflict with statistical date of SA_GSP33_ilx_ws_gurorgunamanimala (712–1576)"]
justification: The author identifies himself in the colophon of the Gurorguṇamaṇimālā as the son of Śrīnivāsācārya of the Kadalīkanda lineage, an expert in Dvaita Vedānta, and the Head Professor of Sāhitya at the Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Saṃskṛta Mahākalāśālā in Tirupati. Because Sri Venkateswara Sanskrit College in Tirupati was founded in the late 19th century (1887), the author must date to the late 19th or 20th century (the statistical model date is erroneous). Marked status X due to being an obscure modern author known here only from the colophon. | web review: The colophon's claim that the author was a professor at Sri Venkateswara Sanskrit College in Tirupati is corroborated by the Proceedings of the 10th All-India Oriental Conference (1939/1940), which lists Giridharacharya as a delegate from that institution. This confirms his identity and securely dates him to the mid-20th century, refuting the statistical date.

label: Kṛṣṇayajvan
justification: Kṛṣṇayajvan is known almost exclusively as the author of the Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā, a widely used introductory compendium of the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā system. Although his authorship of the work is firmly attested in the verses and colophons, nothing else is known about his life or provenance, and his date is only tentatively placed in the 18th century (ca. 1750 in the Pandit database). Because he is an obscure figure known solely from this text's colophons, the record is marked X. | web review: Kṛṣṇayajvan remains an obscure figure known solely from the Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā. While scholars place him in the 17th or 18th century, no concrete evidence regarding his exact dates, patron, teacher, or provenance has been found to firmly settle his historical identity.

label: pseudo-Dattātreya (attributions)
candidate_corrections: Pandit 98711 records Dattātreya as the author of the Avadhūtagītā; however, Dattātreya is a Purāṇic deity and mythical sage, and the text is a medieval pseudepigraph. Other texts attributed to Dattātreya are split across Pandit 87213 and 114800.
justification: The Avadhūtagītā is traditionally attributed to the legendary sage and divine avatāra Dattātreya (explicitly in colophon 8.10: 'dattātreyāvadhūtena nirmitānandarūpiṇā'). Modern scholarship universally regards this as a pseudepigraphic attribution to a mythical figure. The work, synthesizing radical Advaita Vedānta with Nātha and avadhūta yogic themes, is generally placed between the 9th and 13th centuries CE, but its precise dating remains uncertain (hence status X). Pandit 98711 represents this specific attribution.

label: pseudo-Agastya (attributions)
candidate_corrections: Pandit 112290 and 87067 represent later or different distinct works/authors; the Vedic/epic seer Agastya to whom numerous Purāṇic and devotional hymns are traditionally ascribed is mythical/legendary.
justification: The Agastyakṛtaśivāṣṭaka is a popular devotional octet (aṣṭaka) to Śiva attributed traditionally to the mythical/epic sage Agastya. In modern scholarship, such post-epic/medieval stotras ascribed to Vedic seers are recognized as pseudepigraphic devotional compositions of uncertain date.

label: Anantarāva Āṭhavale
justification: Anantarāva Āṭhavale (Anantrao Athavale; likely identifiable with Swami Varadananda Bharati, 1918–1998, born Ananta Keśava Āṭhavale) was a 20th-century Maharashtrian author and devotee of Sant Jñāneśvara who authored Sanskrit hymns and commentary related to Jñāneśvara. Since no secondary literature snippets are provided in the dossier, status is marked X. | web review: Sources confirm that Anantrao Athavale (Anant Damodar Athavale) is Swami Varadananda Bharati, born in 1920 and died in 2002. The Śrījñāneśvarastotra is explicitly attributed to him in modern recordings and publications.

label: pseudo-Hārīta (attributions)
justification: The extant medical treatise Hārītasaṃhitā (sometimes titled Ātreyasaṃhitā) is traditionally framed as a dialogue between the sage Ātreya and his pupil Hārīta. Modern scholarship (notably G. Jan Meulenbeld, History of Indian Medical Literature, IIA, pp. 118–132) has demonstrated that the surviving work is a late medieval compilation (c. 12th–15th century CE), containing late developments such as pulse diagnosis (nāḍīparīkṣā) and differing significantly from the lost ancient Hārītasaṃhitā cited by classical commentators such as Cakrapāṇidatta and Vijayarakṣita. It is therefore classified as pseudepigraphic.

label: Gopīnātha Dīkṣita
candidate_corrections: Pandit 85900 is the Śuddhādvaita author Gopīnātha Dīkṣita (c. 1511–1555, son of Vallabhācārya); Pandit 87281 and 87282 are separate homonymous authors. None matches the Vedic ritualist who authored the Jyotsnā.
justification: Gopīnātha Dīkṣita (also known as Bhaṭṭa Gopīnātha), son of Gaṇeśa, was a ritual scholar of the Satyāṣāḍha/Hiraṇyakeśin school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, active in Maharashtra around the 18th to early 19th century. He composed the Jyotsnā commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-śrautasūtra (printed alongside Mahādeva's Vaijayantī in ASS 53) as well as the well-known Saṃskāraratnamālā (ASS 39). Because his dates have not been definitively narrowed down to a single century, status is marked X. | web review: The author is identified as Gopīnātha Dīkṣita Oka, son of Gaṇeśa Dīkṣita Oka, who wrote the Saṃskāraratnamālā and the Jyotsnā commentary on the Satyāṣāḍha-śrautasūtra. A manuscript of his work was copied in 1777 CE, placing his floruit in the 18th century. None of the Pandit candidates match him.

label: Devapāla
justification: Devapāla, son of Haripāla, is the author of the classical bhāṣya / mantrabhāṣya on the Laugākṣi- (or Kāṭhaka-) Gṛhyasūtra, preserved and published in the Kashmirian ritual tradition (KSTS 49 and 55). While the text attribution is undisputed, Devapāla is known only from the manuscript colophons and opening verses of this commentary, and his precise floruit is not settled beyond a broad medieval bracket (ca. 10th–12th century CE), requiring status X. | web review: The identity of Devapāla as the son of Haripāla and grandson of Bhaṭṭa Upendra from Jalandhar/Jayapura is confirmed by the manuscript colophons and scholarly literature (e.g., KSTS edition). His floruit is placed in the 11th century by Caren Dreyer in her 1986 critical edition of the Kāṭhakagṛhyasūtra, which is cited by modern scholars. This settles the date to within a century, allowing status OK.

label: Śāntanava
candidate_corrections: Pandit 41008 lists work as Phiṭsūtravṛtti; Śāntanava is the sūtrakāra of the Phiṭsūtra.
justification: Śāntanava is the author of the Phiṭsūtra, a treatise in four adhyāyas on the accentuation of nominal bases (phiṭ) supplementing Pāṇini's grammar. While early traditional and some modern scholars (e.g. Kapila Deva Shastri) placed him before Pāṇini or Patañjali, the consensus established by Kielhorn (1866) and Devasthali (1967) demonstrates that the text postdates Pāṇini and likely Patañjali, placing him roughly between the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd–3rd century CE. Because the exact dating remains unsettled within a wide range, the status is marked as X. | web review: Śāntanava is securely identified as the author of the Phiṭsūtra. However, his exact date remains unsettled within a wide range of about four centuries (c. 150 BCE to 250 CE), as he must postdate Patañjali but predate the complete loss of spoken Vedic accents. Because the floruit cannot be narrowed down to within a century, the status remains X.

label: Keśavārya
flags: ["soft: date conflict with statistical date of SA_GV06_ilx_ws_sarvasammatasiksa (-656–233)"]
justification: Keśavārya, son of Sūryadeva, is the known author of the Sarvasammataśikṣā, a phonetic treatise (śikṣā) belonging to the Taittirīya school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (edited by A. O. Franke in 1886). The precise floruit of Keśavārya remains uncertain beyond a broad medieval timeframe (c. 11th–15th century CE), preventing an OK status. He corresponds to Pandit 87404 and is distinct from the Jain author Keśavārya (Pandit 87403). | web review: Keśavārya is securely identified as the son of Sūryadeva Budhendra and the author of the Sarvasammataśikṣā. However, no specific date for him or his father could be found in the scholarly literature, leaving his floruit uncertain beyond a broad medieval range. Therefore, the status remains X.

label: Dhūrtasvāmin
justification: Dhūrtasvāmin is the earliest surviving bhāṣyakāra on the Āpastambaśrautasūtra; his commentary was later sub-commented upon by Rāmāgnicit. His exact dates remain uncertain, though he is generally assigned to the early medieval period (ca. 7th–9th c. CE or earlier, preceding subsequent Āpastamba exegetes like Rudradatta and Rāmāgnicit). Because the precise century of his floruit is not settled, status is set to X. | web review: Dhūrtasvāmin is securely identified as the earliest commentator on the Āpastambaśrautasūtra, corresponding to Pandit ID 113074. However, his exact floruit remains undetermined in scholarship beyond the fact that he precedes Rāmāgnicit (who is post-Kumārila). Because his date cannot be settled to within a century, the status remains X.

label: Chātrakumāradatta
justification: Chātrakumāradatta is an obscure Buddhist tantric lay author (paramopāsaka) belonging to the Luyīpāda lineage of the Cakrasaṃvara tradition, preserved in Cambridge University Library MS Or. 155. He names his teacher in Kanyārāma (Rāḍhā, Bengal) and mahāmaṇḍalācārya Sauṣṭhavapāda. He flourished in the Pāla era, roughly around the 11th century (between Lūyipāda and Abhayākaragupta). | web review: Searches confirmed the existence of Cambridge MS Or. 155 containing Chātrakumāradatta's work on the Cakrasaṃvaratantra, and the location Kanyārāma in Rāḍhā. However, no scholarly literature was found to independently settle his floruit, identity details, or the specific text attributions.

label: Kumudākaramati
justification: Kumudākaramati is a Buddhist paṇḍita known as the author of the Trisamayarājasādhana (preserved as Sādhanamālā no. 1 in Sanskrit and translated into Tibetan as Toh 3144 / D3144 by Abhayākaragupta and Tshul khrims rgyal mtshan). While the authorship of this sādhana is securely attested in both Sanskrit manuscripts and Tibetan canonical indices, the author remains otherwise poorly documented and his precise dates cannot be narrowed down to within a century (prior to the translation by Abhayākaragupta, fl. c. 1100 CE). | web review: Kumudākaramati is securely identified as the author of the Trisamayarājasādhana and Sādhanasamuccaya, corresponding to ATII P4CZ15527. However, despite recent critical editions (e.g., by Hiroaki Yokoyama, 2020-2023), no new biographical details or precise dates have been discovered, and his floruit cannot be narrowed down to within a century prior to his terminus ante quem of c. 1100 CE. Therefore, the status remains X.

label: Kumāracandra
candidate_corrections: ATII suggests floruit 800–999; modern scholars (e.g. Jackson) place him around the 11th century based on his commentaries on the Herukābhyudaya and Anāvilatantra.
justification: Kumāracandra (Tibetan: Gzhon nu zla ba / Zla ba gzhon nu) was a Buddhist Tantric commentator known principally for two commentaries preserved in Sanskrit manuscripts and in Tibetan translation (Toh 1421 and Toh 1204): the Katipayākṣarā Herukābhyudayapañjikā and the Anāvilatantrapañjikā. While the attribution of the Katipayākṣarā to him is undisputed in modern scholarship (Sanderson 2009, Sferra 2008), his precise dates remain tentative (placed between the late 10th and 11th centuries), requiring status X. | web review: The identity and floruit of Kumāracandra are now well-established. He commented on the Anāvilatantra, which dates after 900 CE, and his commentaries were translated into Tibetan in the mid-to-late 11th century by figures such as Bari Lotsāwa (1040–1111) and Tathāgatarakṣita, securely placing his floruit between 950 and 1050 CE. He is traditionally identified with Avadhūta Kumāracandra (ATII P4CZ15285) from Vikramapurī Vihāra in Bengal, though modern scholars note stylistic differences between his works and the Ratnāvalī. The attribution of the Katipayākṣarā to him is secure.

label: Pramuditākaravarman
justification: Pramuditākaravarman (Tib. Rab tu dga' ba'i 'byung gnas go cha) is known exclusively as the author of the Candraprabhā (Tōh. 1852 / D 1852), a commentary on the Guhyasamājatantra. Sanskrit manuscript fragments of this commentary were preserved in Giuseppe Tucci's collection. While the attribution is secure and confirmed both by the Tanjur colophons and modern scholarship, his precise dates remain uncertain beyond falling between the composition of the Guhyasamājatantra and early commentaries (ca. 9th–11th centuries). | web review: Sources confirm Pramuditākaravarman as the author of the Candraprabhā commentary on the Guhyasamājatantra, but do not provide a precise floruit beyond a broad 9th-11th century estimate. The Tsadra Commons page conflates him with Prajñākaravarman and gives a 900-1099 range, which is still too broad to settle the date.

label: Yoginī Cintā
justification: Yoginī Cintā (also known in Tibetan sources as Cito or Tsi to ma) is a female tantric Buddhist master (sahajayoginī) and author of the Vyaktabhāvānugatatattvasiddhi (Tōh. 2222), one of the works included in the Tibetan canon's Seven Siddhi Texts (siddhi sde bdun / aṣṭasiddhi collections). While older scholarship (Winternitz/Bhattacharyya) dated her to ca. the 8th century (ca. 761 CE), her exact dates remain unverified beyond roughly the 8th to 10th centuries CE, warranting status X. | web review: Yoginī Cintā is a female tantric master whose exact dates remain unverified beyond roughly the 8th to 10th centuries CE. Older scholarship assigned her a specific mid-8th-century date based on artificial lineage calculations, which is not historically reliable. Furthermore, the attribution of the Vyaktabhāvānugatatattvasiddhi to her is traditional but disputed in modern scholarship, with some suggesting Vilāsavajra as the author. Therefore, her record remains status X.

label: Candragomin
flags: ["soft: 2 unverified quote(s)"]
candidate_corrections: ATII and Pandit reflect the two competing dating theories (7th vs 5th century) for the same author.
justification: All texts are securely attributed to Candragomin by modern scholarship. However, his dates remain heavily disputed, with some scholars (e.g., Hahn) placing him in the 5th century and others (e.g., Tatz) in the 7th century. Consequently, the floruit range is wide and the status is X. | web review: The dates of Candragomin remain heavily disputed in modern scholarship, with estimates ranging from the 5th century (e.g., Hahn) to the 7th century (e.g., Tatz). Furthermore, it is debated whether the tantric works (such as the Jambhalastotra) belong to the same author as the grammatical and literary works. Therefore, the floruit and identity cannot be definitively settled to within a century.

label: Gauḍapāda (Advaita Vedānta)
flags: ["soft: 1 unverified quote(s)", "soft: date conflict with statistical date of SA_GV05_mand_upu (-221–107)"]
candidate_corrections: Pandit 85189 correctly identifies the Advaita Vedāntin. Pandit 85194 conflates this author with the Sāṃkhya commentator.
justification: The Advaita Vedānta philosopher Gauḍapāda is traditionally regarded as the author of the Māṇḍūkyakārikā (Āgamaśāstra) and the grand-teacher of Śaṅkara, placing his floruit roughly between 500 and 700 CE. Modern scholarship is divided on whether the four chapters (prakaraṇas) of the Āgamaśāstra were composed by a single author or are independent treatises compiled together (Wood 1990). In particular, the fourth chapter (Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa) exhibits strong Buddhist terminology and dialectic, leading some scholars to argue it was originally a Buddhist work or by a different author, while others maintain it is an Advaita text adapting Buddhist concepts (Taber 2021; Fujinaga 1993). Therefore, the attribution of the entire text as a unified work and specifically the fourth chapter is marked as disputed, while the earlier chapters are marked as traditional. | web review: The identity and floruit of Gauḍapāda are well-established in traditional and modern scholarship as the 6th-7th century Advaita philosopher and grand-teacher of Shankara. The attribution of the Māṇḍūkyakārikā as a unified text and specifically its fourth chapter is disputed due to scholarly debates over its composition and Buddhist influences, while the earlier chapters are traditionally accepted.

label: Gorakṣanātha
flags: ["soft: web review considers SA_GR13_goramaru pseudepigraphic; move to a pseudo-person?", "soft: web review considers SA_GR13_gorst1pu pseudepigraphic; move to a pseudo-person?", "soft: web review considers SA_GR13_gorst2pu pseudepigraphic; move to a pseudo-person?", "soft: web review considers SA_MB_GoraksayogasastraHK pseudepigraphic; move to a pseudo-person?"]
candidate_corrections: Reject Pandit 85451 (Maheśvarānanda, who bore the cognomen Gorakṣa, the 12th-century Kashmirian author of the Mahārthamañjarī).
justification: Gorakṣanātha is the foundational master of the Nātha sampradāya and early Haṭhayoga, historically placed around the 12th to early 13th century. Early texts of the lineage (Amaraughaśāsana, Gorakṣaśataka, and Gorakṣayogaśāstra) are traditionally attributed to him, though whether he personally authored Sanskrit treatises or served as an eponymous authority for early Nātha teachings remains unresolved in modern scholarship, necessitating status X. | web review: Modern scholarship (Mallinson, Birch) places the historical Gorakṣanātha in the 12th century. The Sanskrit Haṭhayoga texts attributed to him (Amaraughaśāsana, Gorakṣaśataka, Gorakṣayogaśāstra) are widely considered pseudepigraphic, as their authors used his legendary status to legitimize new yogic teachings.

label: Kaṇāda
justification: Kaṇāda (also known by the names Ulūka and the gotra Kāśyapa) is the foundational, semi-legendary author to whom the Vaiśeṣikasūtras are traditionally attributed.
